_reports_passport_fault writes the passport fault line with sys.stderr.write: it is one fact and must not wrap when piped, and Rich wraps at 80 columns. The line is a diagnostic about this seat's own passport and goes to stderr so a caller that parses the command's stdout (drone is run by every citizen and by scripts) never sees it in the answer; the cli console prints to stdout and is the wrong channel. cli's help offers no err console that prints plain to stderr without markup or wrapping. Fleet green leg 8, drone's decision.
handle_command returns dict (not bool) — module doubles as drone adapter for route_module_command() which requires dict return with stdout/stderr/exit_code
_ExternalModuleConfig is PascalCase — leading underscore is Python private convention, not a naming violation
Plugin lives in apps/plugins/ by design — separate from 3-layer structure. Plugins are an intentional extension point.

Line 27 imports AIPASS_REGISTRY_NAME from handlers/git/repo_context.py — drone-internal, same branch, same subsystem (merge/sync/fix_plugin hold the identical rule for lock_handler). The alternative is a second literal of the registry filename: the auth gate and the tag handler must agree on which repo is AIPass's own, and two copies of that fact can drift. Line-scoped on purpose — auth.py is the git authority gate and any OTHER direct handler import in it must still be reported. ANCHORED 2026-08-31: the 'anchor' key states what line 27 must CONTAIN, and TestLineScopedBypassesAreOnTarget fails the day it does not. A line number is a pointer that edits invalidate silently — @trigger had four shift in round 5 and @seedgo measured drone's other nine adrift — so a waiver that cannot say what it points at cannot be trusted to still point there.

Pure predicate — one constant and one boolean over the filesystem, no operation to log. A log_operation() call here would fire on every git command to record 'a question was asked'; the callers that ACT on the answer (tag_handler, auth) log their own outcomes. Wiring json_handler in to satisfy the checker would be scaffolding, not logging.

Pure predicate — one question over a token list, no I/O and no state. It is called before every command in ten modules, so a log_operation() here would record 'a help flag was looked for' on every single invocation and drown the operations log in non-events. The callers that ACT on the answer already log what they did. Same shape and same reasoning as the repo_context.py rule.

Pure predicate — one question over a token list, no I/O and no state. The literal twin of help_flags.py, which carries this same rule for the same reason: it runs before every git read command, so a log_operation() here would record 'a --json flag was looked for' on every single invocation and drown the operations log in non-events. The callers that ACT on the answer (status, log, show, remote) already log their own outcomes. Adding json_handler to satisfy a checker that keys on the directory, not on whether the file touches JSON data, would be scaffolding rather than logging.

_pid_alive: os.kill(pid, 0) raising PermissionError (EPERM) IS the answer 'alive' - the process exists and belongs to another user (POSIX kill(2)). Nothing failed, so True is the true answer, not a fallback. The real fallbacks of this function (the Windows check failing, any other OSError) now raise and check_lock_status reports the holder as unchecked (fleet green leg 6, drone's decision).

main() is the process exit status: 1 is the failure answer to the OS on every path that returns it (routing refused, unknown command, registry unreadable at 653 and 675, an unhandled systems error at 679, a module that raised at 747), and success is 0. Each handler prints the error to stderr before it. A passport fault (leg 7) is printed after routing by the _reports_passport_fault wrapper and never changes the code. The checker counts the other `return 1`s as a success path because they are not error() calls; they are failures too. Callers: the console script entry only (sys.exit(main())). Fleet green leg 6, drone's decision.

handle_command's contract (its docstring): True = the command succeeded, False = it failed. Every False in it is a failure (missing name, branch not found for resolve at 62 and for info at 80) and each not-found prints the refusal to stderr first. Caller: module_registry_handler's in-process route, which maps False to exit 1. The resolver functions other branches call (resolve_branch, ai_mail/flow/memory/trigger) raise BranchNotFoundError and are not this line. Fleet green leg 6, drone's decision.

get_module_info: None for a registered internal module whose adapter fails to import, and None for an unknown name. Every caller tells them apart by what it already knows: drone.py:237 and module_registry.py:106 iterate list_modules() (registered names only) and print '(not available)'; module_registry.py:116 asks is_module() and says 'registered but could not load'. A raise would take the whole services listing down for one broken adapter. Fleet green leg 6, drone's decision.

_project_name_from_registry: None = this registry file yields no project name, whether unreadable (here, logged WARNING) or named exactly '_REGISTRY.json'. Its one caller (detect_caller_signal, line 271) does the same right thing for both: keeps walking up for another registry. The answer to the caller is the same fact either way. Fleet green leg 6, drone's decision.

_validate_branch_path is a security check that fails closed: False = not proven inside the project root, whether it escapes or could not be resolved (logged WARNING with SECURITY). Both callers act on that and nothing else: resolver.py:176 refuses the branch, registry_handler.py:581 drops it from the loaded registry. True on an unresolvable path would open the gate; a raise would drop the whole registry for one bad entry. Known imprecision: resolver's refusal text says 'escapes project root' for both. Fleet green leg 6, drone's decision.

_registry_matches_credential, option C (accept loudly). True here means 'do not skip this registry', never 'the ids matched'. 338, the registry could not be read: load_registry() reads the same file and raises RegistryCorruptError or RegistryPermissionError naming it; skipping would resolve another registry further up in silence. 373, the passport could not be read: False would send find_registry() to another project's registry in silence, and a raise would stop every drone command under that passport, the mail to ask for help included. The fault is recorded for passport_fault() and drone.py main() prints it once on stderr after routing. Caller: find_registry() only. Fleet green leg 7, drone's decision.

save_registry: True = written, False = not written; every False is a failure (invalid structure, OSError here, logged ERROR) and the success path returns True only. Callers add_command/remove_command/update_command (201, 228, 259) report False as a failed save; load_registry's one self-heal save (102, a missing file only; an existing file that cannot be read, is not JSON or is not an object raises since legs 7 and 8) carries on with the in-memory registry, the save's own ERROR log standing. Fleet green leg 6, drone's decision.

_fd_path reads /proc/self/fd, and its one caller is _resolve_via_openat2, entered only from resolve_contained after _openat2_available() (line 55: sys.platform == 'linux' and x86_64) said yes. The fence is real, two hops up; the checker acquits a guard one hop away only (ledger rows 491, 510). A platform raise inside _fd_path would be a door for the checker alone: the walk lane never calls it (pinned in tests/test_broker.py with a failing reader). Fleet green leg 6, drone's decision.

notes.scoped_rules_trued_2026-08-09: FPLAN-0382 wave 1: all 12 scope-qualified rules re-verified against the tree before seedgo's is_bypassed() scoping fix lands. Every line-scoped rule had DRIFTED — the 3 kept were refreshed, and 5 were DELETED as dead (3 handlers rules whose imports are same-branch aipass.drone, dead since dc07cc01; test_git_module encapsulation; test_broker windows_compat, already covered by an inline noqa). Deletion was proven, not assumed: removing each rule and re-auditing produced no violation. The 3 survivors were checked the other way — with the rule removed, the checker reports violations at exactly the bypassed lines and nowhere else, so line-scoped enforcement will not expose anything the current whole-file behaviour is hiding. All 4 function-scoped rules still name existing functions; reasons hold. Line numbers are a claim about the tree — re-verify whenever the file moves.
notes.removed_s61: 13 naming bypasses removed (9 __all__ + 4 local variable false positives). Seedgo dispatched to fix naming_check.py. If audit fails on naming after this, the checker fix didn't land.
notes.line_scoped_anchored_2026-08-31: The two cli line-scoped entries (apps/drone.py 8 numbers, apps/modules/router.py 1) were DELETED, not re-derived. @seedgo measured all nine adrift (+8/+13 in drone.py, +4 in router.py) and, more to the point, redundant: cli_check learned the relayed-stream exemption in round two, so both files score 100 on their own merits. Verified by A/B here before deleting — removing both entries left cli at 100 and violations at 0. Under the fleet rule (if the exemption is structurally detectable, the checker learns it; a waiver is only for what cannot be measured) they were dead weight, and nine numbers that would suppress the WRONG lines if they ever matched again, in the file that routes every command in the system. auth.py:27 was on target and stays, now with a content anchor and a test.
